title: If You Are Being Arrested
whatToDo:
1. Stay calm. Do not resist or run.
2. Ask: "What is the charge? Which section?"
3. Ask for the arresting officer's name, rank, badge number, and station.
4. Demand to know the grounds of arrest (Section 47 BNSS, 2023).
5. Insist that a relative or friend be informed of your arrest and place of detention (Section 48 BNSS).
6. Ask to meet a lawyer of your choice — you have this right during interrogation, not just after.
7. If poor, ask for free legal aid through NALSA/DLSA (helpline 15100).
8. Insist on being produced before a magistrate within 24 hours of arrest (Article 22(2) of the Constitution, Section 58 BNSS).
9. Do not sign any document you do not understand. Do not confess under pressure.
10. Carry your identity proof. Ask for a copy of the arrest memo.
whatToSay: "I am willing to cooperate but I want to know the grounds of my arrest, the officer's identity, and to contact a lawyer. I will not answer substantive questions until I have consulted counsel. I do not consent to any confession."
whatNotToDo:
- Do not resist, run, or raise your hand against an officer.
- Do not sign any blank or undated paper.
- Do not confess to something you did not do, even under pressure.
- Do not accept tea/water if you suspect it has been tampered with.
- Do not surrender your phone passcode without a court order (you may be asked; legal position is contested — ask for a lawyer first).
- Do not answer incriminating questions without your lawyer present.
whatToKeep:
- Aadhaar / photo ID.
- Phone number of one trusted relative and one advocate.
- Name & number of NALSA helpline: 15100.
- Any prescription medication you need.
- A small amount of cash.
- Note: the police must make an arrest memo and inform your family — insist on it.
applicableLaw: Article 22(1) & 22(2), Constitution of India; Sections 35, 47, 48, 58, 59 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023 (replacing CrPC sections 41, 50, 50A, 56, 56A, 57). D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) guidelines.
authority: Local police station; Judicial Magistrate First Class; State Legal Services Authority (DLSA).

title: Road / Traffic Accident
whatToDo:
1. Check if you or others are injured. Call 108 (ambulance) first if anyone is hurt.
2. Move to a safe spot. Turn on hazard lights. Do not flee the scene.
3. Note the other vehicle's registration number, model, colour, and driver details.
4. Note the time, location, weather, and road conditions. Photograph the scene, vehicle positions, damage, skid marks, and any injuries.
5. If there are independent witnesses, take their names and numbers.
6. File an FIR at the nearest police station (mandatory for injury or death; recommended for major damage).
7. Inform your motor insurer within 48 hours. Note the claim reference number.
8. If the other driver is unknown or fled (hit-and-run), file an FIR with whatever details you have; the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT) can still award compensation.
9. For compensation without long litigation, file before the MACT (or the Claims Tribunal Online facility where available).
10. Seek medical examination even if you feel fine — internal injuries may surface later.
whatToSay: To police: "I wish to report an accident at <location> on <date/time>. My vehicle is <reg no.>. The other vehicle is <reg no.>. There is/is no injury. I request an FIR be registered. I have photographs and witness details."
whatNotToDo:
- Do not leave the scene until the police arrive or FIR formalities are done.
- Do not admit fault at the scene — that is for the investigation and insurer to decide.
- Do not settle verbally for cash without a written note, especially if anyone is hurt.
- Do not refuse medical examination.
- Do not let the other driver leave without noting the registration number.
whatToKeep:
- Driving licence, RC book, insurance certificate, pollution certificate.
- Photos of the scene, vehicle damage, and injuries.
- Witness names and phone numbers.
- FIR copy / FIR number.
- Medical reports and bills.
- Insurance claim reference.
applicableLaw: Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (Sections 132, 134, 161, 166). Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 Sections 105, 106, 281 (replacing IPC sections 279, 304A, 337, 338). Hit-and-run compensation scheme under MV Act.
authority: Local police station; Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT); Regional Transport Office (RTO); insurance company.

title: Domestic Violence
whatToDo:
1. If you are in immediate physical danger, call 100 (police) or 181 (women helpline) or 112.
2. Leave the house with children if you must — your safety comes first. Go to a trusted relative, friend, or a women's shelter.
3. Record evidence if safe: photos of injuries, threatening messages, call logs, witness statements. Get a medical examination (MLC) at a government hospital — it is free and admissible.
4. File a complaint at the nearest police station or the Women's Cell. You can file an FIR for cognizable offences (cruelty by husband/relatives — BNS Section 85; outraging modesty — BNS Section 74; rape including by spouse — BNS Section 63 in defined circumstances).
5. Approach the Protection Officer (PO) of your district to file a Domestic Incident Report under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act (PWDVA), 2005. The PO helps you get protection orders, residence orders, custody, maintenance, and compensation — all civil, fast, and free.
6. Ask the magistrate for a protection order restraining the abuser from contacting you or entering your shared home.
7. Seek free legal aid through DLSA (helpline 15100) — you are entitled regardless of income.
8. Keep an emergency bag ready: ID, cash, medication, children's documents.
whatToSay: To police/PO: "I am <name>, living at <address>. My husband/relative <name> has <describe the act>. I want an FIR registered under BNS Section 85 and a Domestic Incident Report filed under the PWDVA, 2005. I need a protection order and request free legal aid. I have medical evidence and photographs."
whatNotToDo:
- Do not stay if you fear for your life.
- Do not destroy evidence (clothes, messages, photos).
- Do not agree to a verbal 'settlement' without legal advice.
- Do not let anyone convince you that 'this is a family matter' — domestic violence is a crime.
- Do not withdraw the complaint under pressure without your safety guaranteed.
whatToKeep:
- Photo ID (Aadhaar, PAN, voter ID, passport).
- Children's birth certificates and school IDs.
- Marriage certificate / photos / wedding invitation.
- Bank details and any jewellery / cash you can safely carry.
- Medical reports and prescriptions.
- Photographs of injuries and damaged property.
- Threatening messages / call records (screenshots).
- Address and phone of the nearest women's shelter and DLSA.
applicableLaw: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (Sections 18-22). Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 Section 85 (cruelty by husband/relatives, replacing IPC 498A), Section 74 (outraging modesty), Section 63 (rape). Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961.
authority: Local police station; Protection Officer (district); Magistrate; National/State/District Legal Services Authority (15100); National Commission for Women (1091).

title: Cyber Fraud / Online Scam
whatToDo:
1. Immediately call 1930 (National Cyber Crime Helpline) — within the golden hour, banks can often hold the fraudster's account.
2. Report at cybercrime.gov.in (National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal). Select 'Report Cyber Crime Against Women/Child' or 'Report Other Cyber Crime'.
3. Freeze the money: call your bank's fraud line, ask to block your card/UPI, and request a hold on the beneficiary account. Note the complaint reference numbers.
4. Preserve all evidence: screenshot the fraudulent messages, emails, ads, UPI IDs, account numbers, and call logs. Do not delete anything.
5. File an FIR at your local cyber crime cell / police station. Cite BNS Section 318(4) (cheating), 319, 336, and the IT Act, 2000 Sections 66C (identity theft), 66D (cheating by personation).
6. Change passwords of compromised accounts; enable two-factor authentication.
7. Warn your contacts — fraudsters often use stolen accounts to scam others.
8. If the fraud is on a marketplace/app, report to that platform too.
9. Monitor your credit report (CIBIL) for unauthorised loans taken in your name.
whatToSay: To 1930 / cybercrime.gov.in: "I am <name>. On <date/time> I was defrauded of ₹<amount>. The fraudster's UPI/account is <number>, name <name>, phone <number>. I have screenshots and transaction reference <UTRR>. I request the beneficiary account be frozen. I will file an FIR at <station>."
whatNotToDo:
- Do not pay any 'recovery fee' — that itself is a scam.
- Do not delete the chat or the messages.
- Do not engage further with the fraudster.
- Do not click any link they send 'to refund you'.
- Do not share OTPs, even if they claim to be from your bank.
- Do not delay — speed matters for freezing money.
whatToKeep:
- Screenshots of all chats, ads, and emails.
- Bank statement showing the fraudulent transaction + UTR.
- The fraudster's phone, UPI ID, and account number.
- Complaint reference numbers from 1930 and cybercrime.gov.in.
- FIR copy / CSR number.
applicableLaw: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 Sections 111, 318, 319, 336, 338, 340. Information Technology Act, 2000 Sections 43, 66, 66C, 66D, 66F. Reserve Bank of India (RBI) limited liability guidelines for unauthorised electronic transactions.
authority: National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in); Cyber Crime Helpline 1930; local Cyber Crime Cell; bank's fraud desk; RBI Ombudsman for unresolved bank disputes.

title: Child Abuse / Child in Distress
whatToDo:
1. If a child is in immediate danger, call 100 (police), 1098 (CHILDLINE), or 112.
2. Move the child to safety. Do not confront the abuser in a way that endangers the child.
3. Believe the child. Listen without leading questions. Reassure them it is not their fault.
4. Do not bathe the child or change their clothes — physical evidence may be needed.
5. Take the child to a government hospital for a medical examination (free, admissible).
6. Report to the police. Mandatory reporting applies under POCSO Section 19 for everyone who knows of sexual abuse of a child.
7. File under POCSO Act, 2012 (sexual offences against children) and/or Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 (care & protection). For online abuse, also report at cybercrime.gov.in.
8. Contact the District Child Protection Unit (DCPU) and Child Welfare Committee (CWC) for shelter, counselling, and care.
9. Seek free legal aid via DLSA (15100) and support from CHILDLINE (1098).
10. Preserve evidence: messages, photos, the child's statement (audio/video if safe).
whatToSay: To police/CWC: "I am <name>. A child aged <age> at <location> has disclosed <abuse>. The suspected abuser is <name/details>. I request an FIR under the POCSO Act, 2012 and the child's production before the Child Welfare Committee. The child needs medical care and counselling. I have preserved the following evidence: <list>."
whatNotToDo:
- Do not question the child repeatedly — that can contaminate testimony.
- Do not confront or warn the abuser — this can endanger the child.
- Do not bathe the child or wash their clothes.
- Do not make the child repeat the story to multiple people.
- Do not keep the abuse 'within the family' — reporting is mandatory under POCSO.
- Do not blame the child or treat them as complicit.
whatToKeep:
- The child's Aadhaar / birth certificate / school ID.
- Medical examination report.
- Any messages, photos, videos, call logs.
- Names and statements of witnesses.
- FIR number and POCSO case details.
- Contacts of CWC, DCPU, CHILDLINE (1098), DLSA (15100).
applicableLaw: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012. Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015. Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (various sections for non-POCSO offences against children). IT Act, 2000 for online abuse. RTE Act, 2009 for school-related violations.
authority: Local police (Women & Child Protection Unit); CHILDLINE 1098; Child Welfare Committee (CWC); District Child Protection Unit (DCPU); NCPCR (National Commission for Protection of Child Rights).

title: Medical Emergency
whatToDo:
1. Call 108 (ambulance) or 102. If no ambulance, use any vehicle — hospitals cannot refuse emergency patients (SC in Pt. Parmanand Katara case).
2. Stay with the patient. Keep their airway clear; if trained, do CPR. Stop bleeding with pressure.
3. Carry the patient's ID, medication list, and any known allergies. If diabetic, suspect low sugar.
4. At the hospital emergency, the hospital must provide first aid/stabilisation before any payment or paperwork (Clinical Establishments Act; SC guidelines).
5. Demand a Medico-Legal Case (MLC) register entry if the emergency is from an accident, assault, poisoning, burn, or suspicious cause — this protects the patient legally.
6. Insist on a discharge summary and all investigation reports before leaving.
7. Keep all bills and receipts — insurance and compensation depend on them.
8. For organ donation or end-of-life decisions, the patient's prior written directive and family consent matter; consult a doctor and lawyer.
whatToSay: To ambulance/hospital: "Patient is <name>, <age>, <complaint> since <time>. Known allergies/medications: <list>. Pick up from <location>. This is / is not an MLC. Please stabilise first — payment is being arranged. Register an MLC entry."
whatNotToDo:
- Do not delay transport waiting for a 'perfect' ambulance.
- Do not give the unconscious patient food or water.
- Do not move a suspected spinal-injury patient unnecessarily.
- Do not leave the hospital without the discharge summary and reports.
- Do not pay cash without a receipt.
- Do not refuse an MLC entry if the cause is accidental or assault — it protects you.
whatToKeep:
- Patient's Aadhaar / ID.
- List of medications and allergies.
- Health insurance card / policy number.
- Emergency contact numbers.
- All bills, receipts, discharge summary, and investigation reports.
- MLC register number.
applicableLaw: Article 21 of the Constitution (right to life). Supreme Court in Pt. Parmanand Katara v. Union of India (1989) — no hospital can refuse an emergency patient. Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010. Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (medical negligence as deficiency of service). Transplantation of Human Organs Act, 1994.
authority: 108 / 102 ambulance service; nearest government hospital; State Medical Council (for negligence complaints); Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission; State Health Department.

title: Fire Emergency
whatToDo:
1. Call 101 (fire brigade). State the address clearly, nearest landmark, and whether people are trapped.
2. If the fire is small and contained, use a fire extinguisher (PASS: Pull pin, Aim at base, Squeeze, Sweep). Otherwise, evacuate.
3. Alert everyone. Crawl low under smoke. Cover nose and mouth with a wet cloth.
4. Use stairs, never the lift. Feel doors with the back of your hand before opening.
5. Once out, do not re-enter for belongings. Assemble at a safe point and account for everyone.
6. Inform the electricity company to cut supply if electrical fire.
7. Inform your insurance company at the earliest.
8. File an FIR if arson is suspected. For accidental fire, take the fire brigade's report for insurance.
whatToSay: To 101: "Fire at <full address>, nearest landmark <name>. <Number> people are trapped on floor <n>. Smoke is heavy. Please send fire tenders. Electricity supply is / is not cut. Contact person on site: <name, phone>."
whatNotToDo:
- Do not use water on an oil or electrical fire.
- Do not take the lift.
- Do not re-enter a burning building for belongings.
- Do not break windows unnecessarily — that can feed the fire with oxygen.
- Do not delay calling 101 to 'put it out yourself' if the fire is spreading.
whatToKeep:
- Address and landmark clearly posted near the phone.
- Fire extinguisher (serviced annually) and smoke alarm.
- Insurance policy number and emergency contact list.
- A go-bag with ID, cash, medication.
- After the fire: fire brigade report, FIR if arson, photos, bills for insurance.
applicableLaw: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 Section 326 (arson), 279, 336-338. National Building Code of India, 2016 (fire safety). Fire services are a state subject — local Fire Services Act applies.
authority: Fire brigade (101); local police (100); electricity distribution company; insurance company; State Fire Services Department.

title: Natural Disaster (flood, cyclone, earthquake)
whatToDo:
1. Monitor official warnings: IMD (imd.gov.in), NDMA (ndma.gov.in), local administration SMS alerts.
2. Move to higher ground (flood/cyclone) or open ground away from buildings (earthquake). Follow evacuation orders.
3. Carry a go-bag: ID, cash, water, dry food, torch, first-aid, medication, charged power bank, important documents in a waterproof bag.
4. Keep your phone charged and on low-power mode. Inform a relative outside the area of your location.
5. Switch off gas, electricity, and water mains before leaving.
6. Do not walk or drive through flood water — even shallow water sweeps vehicles away.
7. After the disaster, register with the local authority / relief camp for compensation. Keep receipts of losses.
8. For compensation under State Disaster Response Fund / National Disaster Response Fund, file through the district administration.
9. For insurance claims, notify within the stipulated time; keep photos and bills.
whatToSay: To local administration/NDMA: "My family at <address> needs evacuation/relief. We are <n> adults and <n> children. One person needs medication for <condition>. We have / do not have transport. Please advise the nearest relief camp."
whatNotToDo:
- Do not ignore evacuation orders.
- Do not cross flood water on foot or by vehicle.
- Do not take shelter under trees, hoardings, or weak structures.
- Do not use lifts during an earthquake.
- Do not light matches if you smell gas.
- Do not spread rumours — share only official information.
whatToKeep:
- Aadhaar / ID for each family member.
- Cash (ATMs may not work).
- Drinking water, dry food, torch, batteries, first-aid kit, medication.
- Insurance policy numbers.
- Important documents in a waterproof bag: property papers, bank passbook, marksheets.
- Charged phone + power bank.
applicableLaw: Disaster Management Act, 2005. State Disaster Management Authority guidelines. For compensation: State Disaster Response Fund (SDRF) / National Disaster Response Fund (NDRF) norms. Insurance contract terms for private claims.
authority: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA); State Disaster Management Authority; District Magistrate / Collector; NDRF / SDRF battalions; IMD; local municipal authority.
